label: Shemu'el Bet (2 Samuel) — Part 3 — Chapters 13–18
summary_plain: Amnon rapes his half-sister Tamar. Dawid is angry but does nothing. Avshalom waits two years, then kills Amnon. Avshalom flees to Geshur for three years. Yo'av arranges his return through the wise woman of Teqo'a. Avshalom conspires to take the throne — he steals the hearts of the men of Yisra'EL. Avshalom declares himself king at Hevron. Dawid flees Yerushalayim on foot, weeping, head covered. Chushai the Arkite defeats the counsel of Achitofel. Avshalom pursues Dawid across the Yarden. In the forest of Efrayim, Avshalom's hair catches in a terebinth tree. Yo'av kills Avshalom against Dawid's explicit orders. Dawid weeps: O my son Avshalom, my son, my son Avshalom! Would I had died instead of you!
summary_scholarly: The ACR reads from 4QSam-a and the Orit Ge'ez. The Avshalom rebellion (chs 13-18) is the direct consequence of Natan's prophecy: 'the sword shall never depart from your house' (12:10). YHWH's word operates through cause and effect — Dawid's sin with Bat-Sheva produces generational consequences. The rape of Tamar (ch 13) exposes the failure of patriarchal power: Dawid is angry but does nothing, leaving Avshalom to take justice into his own hands. 4QSam-a preserves textual variants in the Avshalom narrative. The Orit Ge'ez provides independent witness to the account. Avshalom's rebellion follows the pattern of contested kingship — he goes to Hevron, the same city where Dawid was first anointed, to declare his own kingship.

key_terms.definition: After Avshalom's death, a new revolt breaks out under Sheva ben Bikhri of Binyamin. Yoav pursues Sheva; a wise woman in Avel negotiates to deliver Sheva's head over the wall to avoid the city's destruction. David returns to his throne but in a weakened, divided kingdom.

David's nephew and chief general — ruthless, effective, loyal to David's survival above David's express commands. He killed Avner, killed Avshalom against David's direct orders, and killed Amasa. At the end of David's reign he supports Adoni-Yah's bid for the throne.

When David returns, Mephiboshet meets him unkempt — unwashed since the day David fled. His servant Tsiva had told David during the flight that Mephiboshet was hoping to regain the kingdom. Mephiboshet denies it. David, unable to determine truth, splits Sha'ul's land between Tsiva and Mephiboshet.

2 Shemu'el 22 — David's psalm of deliverance, essentially the same as Tehillim 18. It opens: 'YHWH is my rock, my fortress, and my deliverer.' It closes with the Davidic covenant affirmation: 'He shows steadfast love to his anointed, to David and his offspring forever.'

2 Shemu'el 23 — a formal list of David's elite warriors. It includes Uriyah the Hittite in the list — the man David had killed. This is the former prophets' honest accounting: the same record that celebrates the kingdom includes evidence of the king's greatest crime.

2 Shemu'el 24: David commands a census of the fighting men. After the census is done, David's heart struck him: 'I have sinned greatly.' YHWH offers three punishments; David chooses three days of plague rather than human enemies. 70,000 die.

The plague-angel stops at Araunah the Jebusite's threshing floor on Mount Moriah. David purchases the site and declares: 'I will not offer to YHWH my Creator that which costs me nothing.' This site becomes the Temple Mount.

The opening of David's psalm in 2 Shemu'el 22: 'YHWH is my rock, my fortress, my deliverer; my Creator my rock, in whom I take refuge, my shield and the horn of my salvation, my stronghold and my refuge, my savior, you save me from violence.' Ten metaphors for covenant protection.

2 Shemu'el 23:1-7 — a formal oracle. David identifies himself as 'the anointed of the Creator of Ya'akov, the sweet psalmist of Yisra'el.' He describes the righteous ruler: 'He who rules over humans justly, who rules in the fear of YHWH, is like the morning light.'

When David returns, Shimei (who had cursed him during the flight) rushes to beg forgiveness. Avishai wants to execute him. David pardons him — but on his deathbed he instructs Shelomoh to deal with Shimei in his own time.

faq.question: Why was David's census sinful?
faq.answer: The covenant law in Shemot 30:12 specified that when the people are counted, each person must give a ransom for their life — 'so that no plague comes upon them when you number them.' The census in 2 Shemu'el 24 did not follow this protocol. Beyond the procedural violation, the deeper issue was what drove it: Yoav's objection suggests it was motivated by pride in military might — wanting to know the size of Yisra'el's army as a measure of David's power, not for covenant purposes. Even David recognized it immediately: 'I have sinned greatly.' The covenant king's strength should be YHWH, not counted soldiers.

faq.question: What is significant about Araunah's threshing floor becoming the Temple site?
faq.answer: The site on Mount Moriah where the plague-angel stopped is where David purchases ground for YHWH's altar. David's declaration — 'I will not offer to YHWH something that costs me nothing' — means the Temple's future site was purchased, not received as a gift. Mount Moriah is also identified in 2 Divrei HaYamim 3:1 as the place where Avraham bound Yitzhak. The Temple Mount thus carries three covenant resonances: the Akeida, the plague-halting altar of David, and the Temple Shelomoh built. The site is not chosen arbitrarily — it is where covenant events have already marked the ground.

faq.question: What does the covenant song of chapter 22 declare about YHWH?
faq.answer: The psalm opens with ten metaphors for YHWH's protective presence — rock, fortress, deliverer, shield, horn of salvation, stronghold, refuge, savior. It then narrates YHWH's violent intervention when David cried out: earthquakes, smoke, fire, darkness, hailstones, thunder, lightning, depths of the sea laid bare. The cosmic imagery describes YHWH entering human history through catastrophic force on behalf of his anointed. It closes with the Davidic covenant affirmation: 'He shows steadfast love to his anointed, to David and his offspring forever.'

faq.question: What does Uriyah's presence in the mighty men list mean?
faq.answer: The list of David's thirty-seven mighty men in 2 Shemu'el 23 ends with 'Uriyah the Hittite.' This man, whom David had murdered, is listed with honor in the official record. The text does not explain the irony; it simply lists him. This is the former prophets' honest accounting: the same record that celebrates the kingdom includes the evidence of its king's greatest crime. Uriyah was loyal, brave, and covenant-faithful — he refused to go home while his comrades fought. He is in the official record because he belonged there.

faq.question: What does David's last words oracle reveal about covenant kingship?
faq.answer: David's last words (2 Shemu'el 23:1-7) are framed as a divine oracle. He describes the ideal ruler: 'He who rules over humans justly, who rules in the fear of YHWH, is like the morning light' — bringing clarity, warmth, life. The oracle is both backward-looking (David's own covenant rule as the standard) and forward-looking (the dynasty's future). The 'morning light' image for covenant kingship becomes the template for YHWH's future anointed.

faq.question: What does the Mephiboshet uncertainty at David's return reveal?
faq.answer: David cannot determine whether Mephiboshet was innocent or whether Tsiva's accusation was true. He splits the land — a compromise that satisfies no one. Mephiboshet's response — 'let him take everything, since my lord the king has come home in peace' — sounds either like genuine gratitude or calculated statement. The text leaves it unresolved. This ambiguity is realistic: covenant loyalty cannot always be verified, and the covenant community must sometimes operate in the face of genuine uncertainty.

faq.question: What does Yoav's career reveal about covenant governance?
faq.answer: Yoav killed Avner in revenge, killed Avshalom against David's direct command, killed Amasa treacherously, and supported the wrong succession candidate at David's end. Yet he was effective and militarily indispensable. David never executed him. On his deathbed, David instructed Shelomoh to deal with Yoav for the bloodguilt David had been unable to address. Yoav illustrates the difficulty of covenant governance: the most effective instrument is sometimes the most morally problematic, and dependency on that instrument can delay justice indefinitely.

faq.question: What does David's choice of plague over human enemies reveal?
faq.answer: YHWH offers three options: famine, enemy pursuit, or plague. David's response — 'let me fall into YHWH's hand, for his mercy is great; let me not fall into human hands' — reflects mature covenant faith. He has experienced YHWH's mercy directly. The choice is not calculation about which punishment is smallest — 70,000 died. It is a declaration about YHWH's character: even in judgment, YHWH is preferable to human cruelty. The plague ends at Araunah's threshing floor before the full period expired — YHWH did relent. David's trust in YHWH's mercy was vindicated.

faq.question: What covenant principle does Shimei's pardon reveal?
faq.answer: David pardoned Shimei on the day of his return to power. The pardon was genuine in the moment but carried a private instruction: on his deathbed David told Shelomoh 'do not hold him guiltless.' The two acts are not contradictory: the oath not to kill Shimei was real and kept. The covenant accountability Shimei bore for cursing YHWH's anointed did not disappear with the pardon; it was transferred to the next administration. David kept his oath while ensuring the underlying justice was not permanently abandoned.

faq.question: What does 2 Shemu'el as a whole say about the Davidic dynasty?
faq.answer: 2 Shemu'el opens with the most transcendent covenant promise in the former prophets (the Davidic covenant) and closes with David purchasing the Temple site through covenant principle. Between these two bookends is a sustained record of human failure: murder, adultery, rape, rebellion, plague. The book's argument is not that David was great and therefore the covenant is real. It is that YHWH's covenant with David was real in spite of David being human. The dynasty survived Avshalom's rebellion and David's own crimes — not because David earned it but because YHWH swore it. The covenant is reliable precisely because it is not based on the human recipient's performance.
